text:
I remember Ati/AMD routinely owning Nvidia, offering not only competitive cards in terms of performance, but cards that were more efficient, quieter and cheaper. Today AMD seems to be completely fine with being just slightly less expensive than Nvidia while having dumped everything else (performance, features, efficiency, driver quality, etc.). It's not difficult to explain why not a single GPU from AMD is represented in the top 10 GPUs in Steam's hardware survey and only two GPUs are in the top 20. 
8GB VRAM can still work, but only if you're willing to accept a significant drop in performance, resolution and quality. Beyond 1080p with high details 8GB are really struggling. Yes, things like DLSS and FSR can compensate, but only so much. The fact that DLSS can turn an otherwise unplayable game into completely playable with 60 FPS or more is impressive, but it's ultimately a trick to fool customers into thinking that they're getting what they paid for. When I pay for a car with 200 HP, I expect there to be an engine delivering 200 HP, not a 50 HP lawnmower engine that's connected to a speaker that goes "WROOOOM! WROOOOM!" like a 200 HP engine.

text: In the past week I've upgraded from a rx 6600 8gb to the rx 9060 xt 16gb for £327.48, delivered the next day and I could not be happier. text:
Okay, I know that this is beating a dead horse, but it's more important now than ever. Guys, inflation over the past decade has been insane with $350 USD today having the same buying power as nearly $500 in 2015. There comes a point where we need to catch up and realize that $350 isn't the same as it was. 

The global economy is still trying to catch up after covid-19, Trump is throwing everything into disarray, and there's uncertainty in component supply, partly due to geopolitical tension between China and Taiwan. 

It becomes a problem of profitability when the parts alone to produce some of these products inches closer and closer to what people still think is a good price. 

This doesn't excuse the shady marketing, but, I mean, it's been the same, "$350 is too much for this performance," for a decade, but the performance has improved for relatively less cost over this time. 

There are certainly markets, such as video games, where the price can remain stagnant because market scale can make up for the reduced profits per unit. GPUs aren't quite like that.

text:
It doesn’t matter how much VRAM you have—once you have enough, more doesn’t magically improve anything. I run all my games at 3440x1440p (72% pixels of 4K) on a GPU with 16GB of VRAM (RTX 5080), and I’ve never seen usage go over 10GB. In fact, the vast majority stay under 9GB, even with DLSS and maxed-out settings.

So when a game like Indiana Jones stutters or struggles and claims it “needs” 16GB+ of VRAM, it’s not about hardware—it’s about poor optimization. Sloppy asset streaming, uncompressed textures, or bloated engines don’t justify high memory requirements. That’s not innovation, that’s bad design.

VRAM isn’t like clocks or raw horsepower—you don’t benefit from "more" unless you're running into a cap. You can always use more performance, but you can't magically make extra memory meaningful if the game doesn’t need it.

I even disagree with Linus on this. It’s not that games are “pushing boundaries” or “demanding more from hardware.” Too often, it’s just laziness, poor cross-team communication, or bloated pipelines. These aren’t cutting-edge technical achievements—they’re just unfinished or poorly optimized projects being patched on the fly.

8GB of VRAM should still be sufficient for 1440p gaming today. If a game struggles to perform within that limit, it's more often a sign of poor optimization than genuine hardware demands. Unless a title is introducing truly advanced rendering techniques or a noticeable leap in visual fidelity, excessive VRAM usage is usually the result of inefficiency. As players, we should be calling that out and holding developers accountable, not normalizing bloated system requirements.

And when I say ''Players'' that includes you, Linus.

text:
​​ @XIIchiron78  People trying to “future-proof” mid-range GPUs are missing the point — these cards aren’t designed to run ultra settings for years. The core architecture becomes the limiting factor long before VRAM does.

Also, just to clarify for the person before you — I never said 8GB is enough for all of 1440p.

I run 3440×1440 ultrawide, which is around 3.4K (UWQHD) and pushes nearly 5 million pixels per frame — that’s about 34% more than standard 1440p (2560×1440, ~3.7 million pixels). When I hit 10GB of VRAM usage at my resolution, it’s fair to assume that standard 1440p would use about 7.5GB, since it renders roughly 25% fewer pixels.

And that’s at ultra settings — which, let’s be honest, isn’t what mid-range GPUs are meant for. If they could handle everything maxed, no one would buy high-end cards.

On top of that, new texture compression technologies from both NVIDIA and AMD are on the way, which will bring VRAM usage down across the board.

In the vast majority of games, 8GB still provides a solid experience at 1080p and even 1440p on medium to high settings. You don’t need ultra settings to enjoy a game.

Now with the 5000 series, it’s a different story — the architecture is far more efficient, and the core is less likely to be the bottleneck before VRAM.

People just need to have realistic expectations. GPU tiers exist for a reason. Yeah, we’re all getting less for more, but crying about 8GB on a mid-range card just doesn’t make sense.

I have a 5080 with 16GB, and even in poorly optimized games like Indiana Jones, I’ve seen VRAM usage go above 10GB — but that’s because the game is flawed, not because that much VRAM is genuinely required.

And yet people are complaining it didn’t come with 24GB… seriously, why? People want both a highend gaming AND workstation GPU for 400$ I mean come on.

text:
​ @tylerstickle2957 The argument isn’t “8GB can’t run games at all.” The argument is that 8GB is already hitting VRAM limitations in modern AAA titles at high textures and RT, and that this situation will only worsen as 2025+ games roll out. Alan Wake 2, Cyberpunk 2077 (RT/Ultra), Dragon’s Dogma 2, The Last of Us Part I, Avatar: Frontiers of Pandora – all can exceed 8GB at 1080p high settings.

These don’t just drop FPS — they stutter, stream textures slowly, or force lower settings.

Several titles now straight-up label 8GB as “Low/Minimum” for high presets. Sure, 8GB can hit 100+ FPS in esports titles or older games, but we're talking about:

AAA next-gen titles

High textures + RT + stable frametimes

No VRAM-swapping to system memory (which causes stutter/fps spikes) If you need to turn down textures or rely on FSR to stay within VRAM limits, that proves the point — the GPU is already at its memory ceiling.  If you’re happy lowering textures and using upscaling to make 8GB work, that’s fine.
But pretending that means 8GB is “future-proof” or not limiting modern AAA games? That’s just ignoring what’s already happening.

text:
As far as I'm concerned this IS a happy day. AMD just handed every PC builder in America the perfect reason to start buying Intel cards, and legitimizing a competitor in the market is a good thing.

A console costs $500 and can play all the modern AAA titles. If I want that on an Nvidia card, that's $500 just for the gpu. If I want it on AMD, that's $400. Intel? For $300 I can get a card that does the job good enough. And the thing is, for $4-500 that's all you're getting from the other guys! You're only getting a card that does "good enough."

Neither of the offerings from AMD or Nvidia at that $4-500 price point is giving you great performance. For that, you have to drop $3000 on the GPU alone! That's what an enthusiast price point looks like. So why spend $500 on "good enough" in a machine that's going to total upwards of $2000 to finish?

For under $900 I can build a full PC that's good enough. And if I'm not shelling out for something actually "good" then why waste money on better than "good enough?"

The generational improvements shrank, and performance tier costs increased with essentially every generation since roughly 2015. An RX 9060 effectively is a 7600, or 6600, or 5600, or 560, ... . 
A 9060 8GB should not exceed around $200, and the 16GB version not $250 - effectively around the price of the Intel ARC. Not just having to buy new but also to spend more just to remain in the same performance tier, is a scam.
I saw it coming though, because while the RX 9070 (XT) are nice, you still pay around $300 more than for the same performance tier of the last generation (RDNA3), and around $375 more than the one before that (RDNA2) - and most people don't even notice or care.

text:
Someone screwed up the AI benchmarks... You don't run directml with nvidia cards, native CUDA (which most AI processes rely on) allows massive performance increases over Intel and AMD that cannot run native CUDA. The directml switch is the only other option without some customized AMD ROCm or Intel VINO setup in a linux distro. A native CUDA setup shows scores/speeds 3-10x faster (depending on AI workload, model, LLM, image gen, etc) vs AMD/Intel with directml.
With my personal testing, AI image generation (SDXL Pony in Win10, 32GB RAM, 5900X, B550) with a 16GB 5060Ti is 20-23 seconds per image versus 180-200 seconds per image using directml with 12GB RX6750XT and 8GB RX7600. Even a 12GB 2060 comes in around 38-42 seconds per image, and a 8GB 3050 is 63-65 seconds per image with native CUDA. The 16GB 5060Ti would likely be a little faster if I had it on a newer setup that can actually make use of the PCIe 5.0, instead of the current PCIe 4.0 on the B550 board.

text:
I think everyone is failing to understand that unlike the CPU space, in the GPU market AMD has a VERY comfortable position. They don't need to be the top dog, and they certainly don't want to rustle too many feathers with the Nvidia execs who MIGHT for once think "oh, we are losing space here? Huh, we should invest more, get out a more competitive product".
 This happens all the time in plenty of industries. You have the high end, mid end and low end brands and they all coexist without competing with each other - and they make sure to not invade someone else's space because it's more profitable that way. It's game theory.
 AMD won't take the shot at being #1 because they know at best they will start a war with Nvidia and they will both make less money, or at worst Nvidia has enough fat in their margins to undercut AMD all around and kick them into irrelevance (and this is not a "Nvidia is better lmao" argument, I'm talking about profit margins).

Every time someone writes something you don't like or disagree with, they must be paid to do it. Of course, because the truth is only what you believe.
Look, with what you've listed, you've confirmed what I wrote. You've also included something that's clearly untrue, like claiming that the issues some Ryzen 9000 processors faced were AMD's fault. Has it ever happened before that people complained about overheat? Think about the P4 during the Prescott era for example, but there are many of such cases.

These are your personal opinions, which are valid as opinions because everyone has the right to judge a company. I have an opposite opinion about them than you . But would these be considered unfair business practices? An unfair business practice is when a company colludes with another to fix prices, for example. Or when they agree, in exchange for money or other benefits, with producers and distributors to prohibit the use or sale of a competitor's products. When they sell a product to a producer (not just to a consumer) while knowing it has defects and then refuse to compensate for damages when the issue arises, suggesting they pass the costs onto customers instead. When they abuse their market position (and also distribute various favors) to force software developers not to optimize for their competitors. The list is long. These are just a few examples. Intel has been condemned (see the EU court ruling against Intel, for example) for some of these practices.
Regarding the Old-timers, you don't need to tell me, as I remember seeing the Spectrum Z81X displayed in store windows, along with those "beautiful" monitors showcasing monochromatic fractals to show people what a PC was for. LOL.
In any case, I've expressed my opinion, cited a few examples, and written for those who wish to inform themselves and verify what I've said. author: @RobCarter04

text:
The VRAM itself is cheap.
But a significant proportion of the cost of adding 8GB more VRAM to the RX 9060 XT comes from the cost of "clamshelling":
Because it has a 128-bit bus, they need to install RAM on both sides of the PCB to get more than 8GB. This makes both the PCB design and the assembly process significantly more complex.
This is still AMD's fault, because they could have just given Navi 44 a 192-bit bus so the 9060 XT could have 12GB without clamshelling, and would also benefit from the higher memory bandwidth.
author: @nathangamble125

text: @petrkdn8224  Good points. It does depend of course on what packages are available because if they are pin compatible then the additional layout costs are effectively zero as long as the increase doesn't impact the control circuitry of an upline component - not so much of an improvement if it's requires an additional package but the "cheap" method of this is to use the same layout and to use lower capacity modules therefore when increasing the RAM it's just a case of changing the modules. The additional power requirements for the extra RAM shouldn't be a problem as most/all of the power controllers in use are easily configurable and likely to support the additional power draw very easily (and the power budget for the RAM is trivial compared to other parts). The change in thermal is definitely a serious consideration though. I don't know how hot GDDR-6 will run but GDDR-5 runs hot at 80°-100° and to prevent damage requires effective heat management and doubling the package capacity is only going to substantially increase the heat generation in a small area requiring much better heat management.

text:
I think it's all about the margin. Let's say AMD wants to have a 70% margin on their products (like Nvidia). When the production costs increases by 15$, they would decrease their margin if they sell the product for just 15$ more. To keep the 70% in this example, the selling price needs to be increased by 50$ (= 15 x (1/0.3)).

Of course, this is not an excuse as they could just accept a lower margin to make the card cheaper but this is how I explain why manufacturers cheap out so much on everything. Because this can also be reversed: Saving 15$ in the production means the product can be sold for 50$ less.

text:
• Overview of the AMD 9060 XT
The AMD 9060 XT is positioned as a value card, potentially outperforming the RTX 5060 Ti 8GB with double the VRAM and a lower price; it comes in three variants: an 8GB version, a base-clocked 16GB model, and an OC variant with higher power draw and boosted clocks. The card is built on the Navi 44 GPU, based on AMD's RDNA4 architecture, which brings improvements in ray tracing and AI performance.

• Performance and Power Consumption Analysis
In 1080p gaming, the 9060 XT performs comparably to the RTX 5060 Ti cards and significantly better than the RTX 5060 non-Ti, outperforming the previous generation 7600 XT by over 30%; however, in some games, the card exhibits higher power draw, necessitating a slightly beefier power supply than AMD's recommendation. While AMD claimed better 1440p gaming performance than the 5060 Ti, tests did not consistently support this claim, and the 9060 XT lags behind in ray tracing performance compared to its Nvidia competitors.

• Concerns and Final Recommendation
AMD faces criticism for potentially misleading marketing practices by releasing both 8GB and 16GB versions under the same "XT" name and for allegedly hindering reviews of the 8GB version; despite improvements in FSR4 and video encoding, AMD is still behind Nvidia in software support, particularly in AI and productivity tasks, leading to a recommendation against the 8GB version of the 9060 XT for those seeking longer lifespan or 1440p gaming capabilities.
